entry.title: Express vs Fastify vs NestJS
entry.content:
Express vs Fastify vs NestJS

  • Express - slow + unstructured.
  • Fastify - fast + unstructured.
  • NestJS - slow + structured.
  • NestJS + Fastify - moderately slow + structured, using fastify.

    For large projects w/ nestjs, using fastify along w/ it does no much performance improvement.

entry.title: 09. Advanced K8s
entry.content:
Advanced K8s (Story Based)

Devops
|-- K8s
    |-- K8s Fundamentals
    |-- Application packaging
    |    |-- helm
    |    |-- charts
    |    |-- values.yaml
    |    |-- chart.yaml
    |    |-- helm repositories
    |-- Gitops
    |    |-- Argo CD
    |    |-- Applications
    |    |-- Application sets
    |    |-- SyncReconciliation
    |    |-- Drift detection
    |    |-- Git as source of truth
    |-- Continuous delivery (CD)
        |-- Progressive Delivery
        |-- Rollbacks
        |-- Automated deployments
  • Without helm
    • Suppose you have multiple services like frontend, backend, postgres, redis, ingress, etc. For each one will have to write deployment.yaml, service.yaml, ingress.yaml, configmap.yaml, secret.yaml, pvc.yaml, etc.
    • This results in 20, 30, 50 yamls… For deploying in different environments like dev & prod we will have to copy that files multiple times.
    • Too much work, duplicate files.
  • With helm
    • Reduced duplication via templates
    • Thus, it is most useful when used in combination w/ template expressions like `` But one can run “helm install myapp” without template expressions just with static data though it is same.(Running above mentioned command is called as installing a helm chart or installing a release.)
    • Template files (with template expressions) are called value files
  • Value files
    • To deploy different kinds of values to different environments (Eg: values-dev.yaml)
    • Avoid duplicated manifests while still maintaining operationBinding to k8s env file, but w/o security.
  • Charts.yaml
    • Addition of it to any folder makes that folder a valid “chart” & makes helm recognise it as one installable package.
    • Running “helm install myrelease my-app” (Installing a helm chart / release)
    • In general, we don’t push charts (folder created w/ charts.yaml) into OCI registries (open w/ charts.yaml) into OCI registries (open w/ charts.yaml). It is just spun on the repos required nodes.
    • But in general, we push to OCI registries same as docker images (Eg: dockerhub, github container registry, Amazon ECR, Google artifact registry, Azure container registry).
  • Multiple charts
    • by having multiple folders ref chart.yaml to install.
  • Third party charts
    • to install, popular reusable packages/charts like prometheus, grafana, etc. redis, postgres, etc.
    • Installing multiple helm charts
      • Helm file
        • used for describing multiple helm releases in one place, or deploying them together & volatile controlling, ordering & shared configuration.
  • Gitops / ArgoCD
    • Subset of DevOps.
    • Focuses on keeping DevOps in sync across teams in large organizations.Git as source of truth
    • A tool used for that is ArgoCD.
      • ArgoCD is a CRD so running in K8s.
      • Entire setup for argo CD as manifests.
      • ArgoCD watches for changes and sunsets them if necessary.Something like protecting dev/main branches in github/gitlab.
      • Argo Project consists of argocd, argo workflows, argo rollouts, argo events.
        • Named after mythological ship Argonauts - Logo of argo is an orange squid.
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (Advanced K8s)

entry.title: SSE vs Websocket
entry.content:
SSE vs Websocket

(Rest api still always better than these open connections)

  • SSE
    • Server sent events.
    • way for server to continuously push updates to a client via HTTP. one-way
    • switch (notification, live dashboard, logs, tokens)
  • Web socket
    • continuous message from both client and server.
  • both use an open connection (not polling). SSE uses HTTP connection. websocket starts as HTTP and then upgraded to websocket protocol where messages are exchanged as websocket frames. (chat apps, game, collab editing)
entry.summary: Understanding diff b/w SSE and Websocket

entry.title: DNS and TLS/SSL
entry.content:
DNS and TLS/SSL

  • DNS
    • Domain naming system
    • assigns registering a static IP of a website and buying a domain name.
  • TLS
    • transport layer security.
    • encrypts data sent b/w client & server.
    • modern version of ssl (secure sockets layer)
    • HTTP + TLS = HTTPS.

entry.title: Load Balancing And Traffic Management
entry.content:
load balancing

  • Round robin
    • load distributed sequentially & evenly across available servers.
    • Eg: 
      upstream backend {
  server app1 : 3000;
  server app2 : 3000;
  }
  • weighted load balancing
    • you weight servers. % wise
    • Eg: 
      upstream backend {
  server app1 : 3000
  weight = 3;
  server app2 : 300
  weight = 1;
  }
    • app 1 get 75% more traffic.
  • least connections
    • traffic to least busy instance.
    • Eg: 
      upstream backend {
  least_conn;
  server app1 : 3000;
  server app2 : 3000;
  }
  • Health check/failover
    • if app dies, traffic moves to app2.
    • Eg: 
      upstream backend {
  server app1 : 3000
  max_fails = 3
  fail_timeout = 30s
  server app2 : 3000;
  }
  • sticky session load balancing 
    upstream backend {
    ip_hashserver ...
    }
upstream backend {
    sticky cookie srv_id expires = 1h;
    server apps ...
    }
    • can be based on IP or cookies etc.
    • not a load balancing algo, but rather a constraint that modifies load balancing behaviour.
entry.summary: Understanding Load Balancing

entry.title: Istio Ingress
entry.content:
Istio-ingress

  • An alternative to nginx ingress.
  • Ingress fundamentals:
    • K8s ingress (needs an ingress controller like nginx, traefik, HAProxy, etc.).
    • Focused on layer 7 (HTTP) routing.
      • Nginx is said to be basic layer 7 routing. Istio is a advanced layer 7 routing b/c it provides much more than nginx through at layer 7, like traffic splitting, canary deployments, retry policies, circuit breakers, mTLS, observability, fault injection.
      • Layers (Comp. Sci network model term)
        • 3 Network models :- OSI Model, TCP/IP Model, Hybrid TCP/IP model.
        • OSI model
          • created by ISO.
          • OSI (Open Systems Interconnection)
          • ISO (Internal Organisation for Standardisation)
      • 7 layers conceptual model. Not used in real world. Used by k8s for theory purpose.
      • 7 model:
        • layer 7 - application
        • layer 6 - presentation
        • layer 5 - session
        • layer 4 - transport
        • layer 3 - network
        • layer 2 - data link
        • layer 1 - physical.
      • layer details:
        • Application
          • user facing
          • HTTP, HTTPS, DNS etc
        • Presentation
          • data format, encryption encoding
          • TLS/SSL, PNG/JPEG, UTF8, ASCII
        • Session
          • connection, session management
          • SMB Session, TLS session, Net BIOS
        • transport
          • End to end communication
          • TCP, UDP, QUIC,
        • network - routing - IP (v4/v6), ICMP
        • Data link
          • communication on same n/w
          • ethernet, wifi, VLAN, MAC address
        • Physical
          • Actual signal transmission
          • copper cables, fibre optic, etc.
      • TCP/IP model:-
        • only 4 layers. used in reality
        • layers include:- Application, transport, internet & n/w access
        • hybrid:
          • has 5 layers
          • application, transport, network, data link, physical
        • other vendor specific layer models that are not commonly used by anyone:
  • Istio-ingress
    • Istio
      • service mesh platform.
      • Contains controlplane (istiod), side car proxies (envoy), traffic management, mTLS, authorization policies, observability, ingress gateway, egres gateway all w/o touching the app.
      • uses istio-ingress gateway which was envoy.
      • envoy, is a proxy that forwards requests, load balancer, TLS termination, metrics, collection, traffic splitting, etc.
  • Other ingress fundamentals
    • north south traffic - traffic to and from outside the app
    • east west traffic - traffic within services of the app internals
    • edge proxy
      • Proxy located at boundary of cluster
      • Does TLS termination, routing, filtering
      • istio ingress gateway is edge proxy
    • load balancer
      • distributes requests across ingress gateway pods.
      • provides stable public IP or DNS name
      • cloud providers create it automatically
    • Request flow:
      • user send req to public domain send
      • DNS resolve domain to public domain
      • load balancer forward req to ingress gateway
      • Gateway evaluate gateway resource
      • Virtual service determine routing rules
      • Request reach service and pods
  • Istio-ingress gateway architecture
    • Istio-ingress gateway deployment
      • K8s deployment in k8s env
      • This deployment has pods, and these pods contain containers called as “envoy container”.
      • Purpose of istio-ingress gateway is to process incoming traffic.
      • deployed within “istio-system namespace.
      • can be scaled independently from main app.
    • Envoy Proxy
      • Name of high performance proxy used by istio. a proxy that’s part of a software called “envoy” developed by “lyft” company.
      • can be used anywhere as a proxy within istio - as sidecar proxy, as a container proxy within pods, etc.
    • Gateway pods
      • pods running envoy.
      • recieve requests from load balancer, apply gateway &, virtual service rules.
      • can be horizontally scaled.
    • Gateway selectors
      • selectors specific to istio
      • enables multiple gateways in one cluster.
    • Can support multiple ingress gateways, per app.
    • Also supports one dedicated gateway per app.
    • GatewayCRD - for deploying istio
    • other gateway resources :
      • hosts on istio (allowed domains) - server (listener definition) open protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, etc.)wildcard host - to match multiple domains like *.example.com, multiple hosts listeners.Gateway binding (associating Virtual Services w/ gateways), Gateway lifecycle.
        • Gateway binding
          • virtual services references Gateway
          • w/o binding routes don’t apply.

            Istio vs nginx

    • istio provides what nginx provides plus service mesh (secure to service communication), mTLS (mutual TLS protecting traffic from service to service), traffic splitting as we want, observability, w/o modifying app code.
entry.summary: Understanding Istio Ingress

entry.title: Load Testing
entry.content:
Load Testing

Testing tests purpose duration typically load
Smoke test verify system works 1-5 min very low
Load verify expected traffic 5-30 min expected production load.
Stress Find breaking point 10-30 min Beyond expected load!
Spike Test sudden traffic surges Few mins Instant large jump
Soak Find long term issues. Hours Normal load
Scalability verify horizontal/vertical scaling load.  
Breakpoint Find exact failure point    
Failure verify recovery from failures    
Chaos Intentionally inject failures    
Capacity Determine max sustainable throughput.    
Resilience test      
Performance regression test      

Load Testing proper table (generally used ones)

  • Test type: Smoke test
    • Purpose :- Verify test setup & basic functionality
    • Typical load vs normal :- 1-5% (10-15 users)
    • Duration :- seconds to 5 min
  • Load Test (must have)
    • Validate performance under expected load
    • load :- 100% (1000 users)
    • Duration :- 15 min to 1 hr
  • Avg. load test
    • Simulate normal business day
    • load :- 50-80% (500-800 users)
    • duration :- 30 min to several hrs
  • Stress test (must have)
    • Find breaking point
    • load :- 120-500% (1200-5000+ users)
    • duration :- minutes
  • Soak/endurance test (sustained test) (must have)
    • Long period check to detect memory leak, connection leak, eta degradation, etc.
    • load :- 70-100% (700-1000 users sustained)
    • duration :- 4-72 hrs (3 days)
    • Capacity test (sometimes )
      • Find max load, while still meeting SLA.
      • SLA :- Service level agreement.
        • A document agreement
        • defines what level of service must be defined & how it is measured.
        • typical metrics include uptime, response time, resolution time, availability.
        • If provide fails to meet targets, SLA may specify penalties, service credits or remedies.
        • eg: if an application’s SLA is
        • availability = 99.9%
        • P95 latency < 300 ms
        • error rate < 0.1%
        • then during load tests these must be maintained.

      • Related terms

        • SLI (Service level indicator)
          • The measurement values
          • Eg: availability, P95 latency, P95 etc
        • SLO (Service level objective)
          • A target for an SLI / engineerng goal
          • Eg: P95 latency < 300ms - over a rolling 30-day period
          • 99% successful requests over 30 days
        • SLA (Service level agreement)
          • customer facing promise
          • involves business/legal consequences
          • P95 latency (Percentile 95 latency)
          • A method to display response times/latency
          • monitoring:
          • Eg: P95 = 300 ms means 95% of requests completed in 300ms or less - 5% faile.
      • load :- Gradually increase from 100% upward.
      • duration :- 30 min - 2 hr
      • Classically stress test but to find near point in compliance of SLA).
  • Scalability test
    • verify scaling behaviour when adding resources.
    • load :- incrementally increasing load.
    • duration :- Hours
  • Volume test :-
    • Test large data size (not user count)
    • load :- normal users, huge data volume.
    • duration :- series
  • Concurrency test :-
    • Many users hitting same resource simultaneously.
    • load :- 100-300% on specific endpoint
    • durations :- minutes
  • Resilience test
    • Behaviour during failure.
    • load :- normal load + injected failures.
    • duration :- 30 min to hours.
  • Recovery test (outage)
    • Recovery after outage/crash.
    • load :- usually after stress/spike.
    • duration :- mins to hours.
  • Peak test (traffic)
    • Validate operation during known peak traffic.
    • load :- 100-150% of highest expected peak.
    • duration :- 30 min to 2 hrs.
    • diff from concurrency testing in a way that enteric apps heavy load is tested.
    • Testing expected real life, high traffic like black friday sale.

Common load testing tools

  • From local m/c to deployed appk6, Apache JMeter (UI based testing - JSlocust (Python scripts based)artillery (yaml based ver &)
  • k6
    • JS based
    • CLI/UI friendly
    • used heavily w/ nestJS + K8s
  • Artillery
    • node native alternative
    • yaml or JS based
  • Apache JMeter
    • GUI based.
    • Manual entry of endpoints.
    • used in banks / large enterprises.
    • legacy
  • locust
    • python based.
    • distributed load testing support.
  • For backend HTTP tools (for quick checks only).
    • wrk, autocannon, hey
    • used for raw benchmarks & not full scenarios.
entry.summary: Understanding load testing

entry.title: LXC
entry.content:
LXC (Linux containers)

  • facts
    • OS-level virtualisation - Not hardware virtualisation.
    • Runs in containers on a host linux kernel.
    • Acts like a small linux m/c.
    • system container (like how docker is application container)
    • Every container has its own - PID namespace, n/w namespace, mount namespace, hostname, filesystem, users (optionally mapped).
    • Containers are isolated using linux namespace and cgroups.
    • linux cgroups enforces following limits on lxc container: RAM, CPU cores, CPU time, disk quota, w/o bandwidth, I/O limits.
    • Has singe host ckernles the kernel. Cannot boot a diff kernel inside lxc like windows on FreeBSD.
    host ubuntu kernel
        |
-----------------
|               |
v               v
lxc 1          lxc 2
(ubuntu)       (debian)
  • Performance (Compared to VMs):
    • Faster startup, lower RAM overhead, better density (more containers per host).
  • Persistence:
    • Stays stuff installed on exe container remains installed even after reboot (less compared to VMs, bcz host kernel is shared).
  • Security:Less vulnerability can affect all containers.
  • Limitation:
    • Linux guests only, cannot use different kernel version, some kernel features/modules depend on host; certain workloads (eg: some K8s or nested containers scenarios) may require extra configuration as workloads in VMs in K8s.
entry.summary: Understanding Linux Containers (LXC)

entry.title: 08. K8s Leanring Continuation
entry.content:
K8s learning (continuation)

  • Linux namespaces
    • helps in isolation
    • types :- PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP
  • cgroups (control groups)
    • for resource control
    • tracks limits of resources
  • Containerd - container runtime
  • OCI (Open Container Initiative)
    • Container standards
    • defines standards for container image & container runtimes
    • Example :-
      • When we build an image, docker creates an OCI-compliant image
      • When we push it, and someone else pulls it, because it is OCI compliant, everyone follows it. The same image works across (docker, containerd, Podman, CRI-O, K8s, etc.)
  • Istio vs port forwarding
    • port forwarding :-
      • Eg: kubectl port-forward svc/my-service 8080:80
      • temporary funnel from my-laptop to pod/svc
      • used for development / debugging / testing
      • Limitations :-
        • Only works while terminal session is running
        • not suitable for real cases
        • no public DNS, no production-grade traffic management, no SSL-TLS termination, no load balancing
      • Istio-ingress gateway :-
      • Expose app to internet permanently
      • Accepts traffic from users, browsers, mobile apps, APIs, etc.
      • Provides routing, TLS/HTTPS, traffic splitting, canary deployments, blue-green deployments, authentication/authorization, observability, rate limiting (w/ extensions)
      • Used when apps are deployed to a real environment like GKE, EKS, AKS, on-prem K8s, etc. Page 15(16)

K8s visualisers

  • K8s dashboard (legacy & deprecated)(GUI)
    • Steps
      • make sure you have helm installed and a running kind cluster. “helm version”, “kubectl config current-context”
      • install K8s dashboard.
      "helm repo add kubernetes-dashboard kubernetes-retired.github.io/dashboard/"
"helm repo update"
"helm install kubernetes-dashboard \
    kubernetes-dashboard/kubernetes-dashboard \
  --namespace kubernetes-dashboard \
  --create-namespace"
      • verify installation : “kubectl get pods -n kubernetes-dashboard”
      • create admin account :-
      # dashboard-admin.yaml

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
    name: admin-user
    namespace: kubernetes-dashboard

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
    name: admin-user

roleRef:
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: cluster-admin

subjects:
    - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: admin-user
    namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
      • Apply this file “kubectl apply -f dashboard-admin.yaml”
      • Generate login token “kubectl -n kubernetes-dashboard create token admin-user”
      • Verify services “kubectl get svc -n kubernetes-dashboard”
      • portforward kong proxy :-
      "kubectl -n kubernetes-dashboard port-forward
svc/kubernetes-dashboard-kong-proxy
8443:443"
      • open https://localhost:8443 & login using token.
      • Every cluster and its associated details will be visible w/o any commands.
  • Headlamp (GUI)
    • install as an app & open it ds.
    • clusters will already be there.
  • k9s (terminal GUI)
    • most used (it seems)
  • lens (GUI) - didn’t try
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (K8s learning continuation)

entry.title: 07. K8s Next Topics
entry.content:
Next topics in k8s

  • Metric server
  • HPA
  • Deployment replicas

Metrics server :-

  • shows metrics for pods & nodes for resource usage
  • Steps :- first install metrics-server from repository, then update metric-server with starter flag. check metrics “kubectl top nodes”, “kubectl top pods -n media-forge-dev”

Importance HPA reads metrics from metrics - server to decide autoscaling.

HPA

  • Write an hpa.yaml with threshold mentioned, beyond which if cpu usage goes, then it increases replicas.

Common K8s commands

  • kind create cluster –name --config
  • in config file: ``` kind: cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 nodes:
    • role: control-plane
    • role: worker …etc ```
  • kind get clusters (see clusters created)
  • kubectl get clusters (see clusters configured)
  • kubectl config get-contexts (see multiple cluster contexts)
  • docker build -t -f Dockerfile (to build image from code changes)
  • kind load docker-image --name
  • kubectl apply -k <path-to-file -kustomization> (to start related pods & clusters. apply kustomization file for each. path you want to spin. eg: for each service)
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (K8s next topics)

entry.title: 06. K8s Points to Remember
entry.content:
K8s app (points to remember)

  • using kind locally
  • we create a control plane node from a docker container.
  • In kind we schedule pods & system related pods both in control plane node. [No taint. In general deployment platforms like GKE, EKS, etc. taints control plane node as “noschedule” to avoid schedule of worker nodes]
  • Commands to apply yamls kubectl apply -f <file-path>
  • command to read applied yamls kubectl get all, kubectl get pods, kubectl get services, ..etc
  • Each time you update yaml, you need to kubectl apply -f filename & then kubectl rollback restart deployment <service-name>
  • Everytime you change any code file we need to nx build <service-name>, docker build t <tag-name> -f <dockerfile-path>, kind load docker-image <tag-name> --name <control-plane-cluster-name>
  • Kustomize config:-
    • Base files are template files.
    • Any config in overlay file overrides settings in base file (eg: overlay namespace overrides base namespace).
  • “kind” is local K8s setup. “kubectl” is cli client to communicate of either kind or GKE or cloud K8s.
  • “Kustomize” is part of kubectl cli
  • Steps to deploy a micro service to local K8s
    1. make sure all rotates mentioned in deployment.yaml readiness & liveness probe exists. (Health api)
    2. Create Dockerfile.tar is in the target microservice file.
      • Eg: 
        From node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
copy package.json pnpm-lock.yaml
RUN corepack enable
RUN pnpm install --ignore-scripts
copy apps/auth-service/dist
CMD ["node", "main.js"]`
    3. Build image -> docker build -t <tag-name> -f <path-to-Dockerfile> . --no-cache
    4. Load into kind cluster kind load docker-image <tag-name> --name=<cluster-name>
    5. Apply new yaml files or restart existing deployment.
      • apply -> kubectl apply -k <path-to-overlays> (via Kustomize for all files)
      • restart -> kubectl rollout restart deployment <service-name> -n <name-space>
    6. Expose ingress port for calling apis:-
      • “kubectl port-forward -n service/ingress-nginx-controller 8080:80"

        To check logs: “kubectl logs deployment/media-service -n " Verify images loaded in kind: "docker exec crictl images"
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (K8s Points to Remember)

entry.title: 05. K8s Cluster Diagram
entry.content:
K8s Cluster Diagram (For Reference)

k8s clusters

Cluster 1 (ex: prod cluster)
|---*Control Plane node A*
|    |---kube-apiserver
|    |    ↳ Authentication
|    |    ↳ Authorization (RBAC)
|    |    ↳ Admission controllers
|    |    ↳ API endpoints
|    |    ↳ Validation
|    |    ↳ watches
|    |---etcd
|    |     ↳ deployments
|    |     ↳ replicasets
|    |     ↳ pods
|    |     ↳ services
|    |     ↳ configmaps
|    |     ↳ secrets
|    |     ↳ namespaces
|    |     ↳ service accounts
|    |     ↳ roles
|    |     ↳ rolebindings
|    |     ↳ clusterroles
|    |     ↳ clusterrolebindings
|    |     ↳ jobs
|    |     ↳ cronjobs
|    |     ↳ daemonsets
|    |     ↳ statefulsets
|    |     ↳ persistent volumes
|    |     ↳ persistent volume claims
|    |     ↳ storage classes
|    |     ↳ nodes
|    |     ↳ events
|    |     ↳ leases
|    |     ↳ Custom Resources (CRD)
|    |---Kubernetes Controller Manager
|    |     ↳ deployment controller (creates/manages replicasets)
|    |     ↳ replicaset controller (creates/deletes pods)
|    |     ↳ job controller
|    |     ↳ cronjob controller
|    |     ↳ statefulset controller
|    |     ↳ daemonset controller
|    |     ↳ namespace controller
|    |     ↳ node controller
|    |     ↳ service account controller
|    |     ↳ endpoint slice controller
|    |     ↳ persistent volume controller
|    |     ↳ replication controller
|    |     ↳ ... many other controllers.
|    |--- kube-scheduler
|    |      ↳ watches pending pods
|    |      ↳ selects worker node
|    |      ↳ resource calculations
|    |      ↳ affinity rules
|    |      ↳ taints & tolerations
|    |      ↳ writes node assignment
|    |---Other controller managers (optional)
|          ↳ load balancer controller
|          ↳ route controller
|          ↳ volume controller
|          ↳ node-controller
|---*Control Plane node B*
|      ↳ ... same as above
↳ Cluster 2 (ex: staging cluster)



Developer machine / CI server
↳ kubectl
↳ kube-adm
↳ Helm
↳ Kustomize
↳ ArgoCD
↳ Terraform
↳ Custom clients

Worker Nodes
↳ Node 1
|  ↳ kubelet
|  |  ↳ talks to api server
|  |  ↳ watches Pod objects
|  |  ↳ starts containers
|  ↳ Container runtime
|  |  ↳ containerd
|  |  ↳ CRI-O
|  |  ↳(formerly docker)
|  ↳ kube-proxy
|  |  ↳ Service Networking
|  |  ↳ iptables
|  |  ↳ IPVS
|  ↳ Running Pods
|    ↳ Pod A
|    ↳ Pod B
|    ↳ Pod C
↳ Node B -> Same structure
↳ Node C -> Same structure

entry.title: 04. K8s Structure and visualization - Part 2
entry.content:
K8s Structure and Visualization

So we’re back to understanding K8s now that we’ve taken a round of understanding the undelining linux basics.

Visualisation

A data center looks like this

Datacenter
|--- Rack
|    |--- Server 1
|    |--- Server 2
|    |--- Server 3
|--- Rack
     |--- Server 4
     |--- Server 5
     |--- Server 6
  • Different servers on diff racks can be part of same Kubernetes cluster.
  • When multiple servers have cost check, certain requirements, they are as associated of k8s, they are then part of k8s cluster. -

K8s terms

  • kubelet
    • small local agent/process
    • Exists on every worker node / control plane node.
    • Make sure containers/pods runs correctly on that m/c.
  • Tasks of kubelet :
    • talk to api server, receive pod assignments, start/stop containers, report node health, report pod status, mounts volume, handle probes.
  • kubectl
    • Pronounced “kyoobe-cuttle” or “kyoobe-control”.
    • Exists on developer laptop / admin m/c / control server.
    • It communicates of kube-apiserver.
  • kube-proxy
    • Kubernetes n/w proxy.
    • exists on every worker node (as daemon/fbg process).
    • It handles k8s n/wing rules inside cluster Eg: Service virtual IPs, load balancing, traffic forwarding, ip tables / ipvs rules.
  • kubeadm
    • K8s admin / bootstrap tool
    • exists on control plane m/c.
    • worker setup m/c
    • used during cluster creation for creating control plane “kubeadm init” & join worker pods “kubeadm join”, etc…
    • Not part of ras running cluster logic instead part of cluster installation / setup tool.
  • kube-apiserver
    • main entry point for k8s cluster. Everything talks to this. Acts like central management api. - Exists on control plane server.
    • Talks to kubectl, kubelet, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd.
  • kube-scheduler
    • chooses which node runs pods. (decision engine)
    • Exists on control plane server. Chooses where worker node try maintains desired state pods.
    • talks to kube-apiserver, worker nodes indirectly.
  • kube-controller-manager
    • Exists on control plane server.
    • Maintains desired state.
    • Talks to :- kube-apiserver, etcd … indirectly.
    • Runs reconciliation loops (loops inside k8s that continuously check desired state vs actual state).
    • eg: desired replica = 3, actual replica = 2. Then create another pod.
  • etcd (etc distributed) (et-see-di)
    • etcd directory / distributed key value db (like redis)
    • store cluster state db.
    • most critical k8s db (source of truth).
    • Exists on control plane servers.
    • Stores :- pods, deployments, services, [as key-value pairs] nodes, secrets, cluster desired state.
    • distributed
      • it is called distributed bcoz multiple etcd servers can work together.
      • eg if multiple control planes with diff etcd, they communicate via a “Raft consensus” algorithm which stores a copy of the cluster state, thus preserving data even if one etcd beads down. (cluster state is not the same as control plane).
  • containerd
    • container runtime (actually runs containers)
    • Exists on worker node.
    • Talks to kubelet through CRI.
  • CoreDNS (Core Domain Name Sys)
    • K8s - Internal cluster dns.
    • lets pods communicate using names. eg: api-service.default.svc.cluster.local. - usually runs as pods on worker nodes.
  • Container Network Interface (CNI)
    • Provide pod networking.
    • Exists as CNI plugins on worker nodes.
    • eg: Calico, Flannel, Cilium.
  • CRI
    • Container runtime interface.
    • Standard interface btw. kubelet (node agent) & container runtime (containerd).
    • Types of communication being done via here include kubelet asking to pull image, start container, stop container, delete container, get container status, etc..
  • CSI
    • Container storage interface.
    • Standard way k8s interact w/ storage systems.
    • Exists on worker node, control plane (occasionally on worker node, control plane)
  • Pod
    • Small deployable unit holding one or more containers together
    • Runs on worker nodes inside container runtime (containerd)
    • Contains 1 or more containers, shared n/w, shared storage, shared localhost
    • e.g., k8s Pod
    • e.g., pod may contain:
      • nodejs API container
      • sidecar logging container, etc.
  • Deployment
    • An object that is stored in etcd (API resource)
    • It is used to keep a permanent record of the desired state of cluster
      • Deployment controller continuously checks actual state against the desired state stored in deployment object (key-value pair) stored in etcd
    • It is generated by k8s from the deployment.yml file (also called deployment manifest) upon running a command like “kubectl apply -f .yaml”
      • It can also be generated from a json file or directly from terminal like “kubectl create deployment –image=”. In such case kubectl itself creates a deployment object based w/ configuration based on kubectl defaults, k8s, defaults by API server generated metadata.
    • Also handles replicas, rolling updates, self healing, rollout history
  • Replica set
    • replica = copy, set = collection
    • it is an API resource (cluster resource) whose instance is stored within etcd
    • Deployment controller, from developer / cr server sense kube controller manages, creates a replica set.
    • Though replicaset obj can be created from a riperi [replica] <missing text: “set”> manifest like deployment
    • it is generally auto-generated by deployment controller. The trigger for creating a replicaset is the appearance or change of deployment object. If expected no. of replicasets are 3 & these objects are 3 & deployment controller creates the extra one.
    • it manages the no. of pods to be kept up
  • Service
    • Objects that defines a service name that also becomes the DNS name inside the cluster (we can also set a static IP for that service that falls in its cluster’s service IP range & must be unique). It is this DNS name kube proxy will use to get incoming calls to BE from FE & then re-route to actual IPs of each pod that gets generated
    • created by user themselves via kubectl (like deployment obj) using a source manifest & stored in etcd
    • Endpoint Slice Controller, watches service objects & Pods, it also creates endpoint slice objects for the service.

      The objects stored in etcd can be multiple in number (eg: multiple service, deployment, replicaset objects, etc.). They can be multiple depending on diff manifests or based on diff namespaces
      eg: → etcd A | ↳ deployments | ↳ dev | ↳ staging | ↳ prod | ↳ services | ↳ dev | ↳ staging | ↳ prod | ↳ pod | ↳ dev | ↳ staging | ↳ prod → etcd B (same thing)

All the etcd’s of the same cluster will shared this segregation based on namespaces & such. (so that if one etcd goes down, others still have data)

  • Ingress
    • meaning → incoming traffic
    • it routes external HTTP / HTTPS traffic into cluster.
    • created from ingress manifest by the user/developer using kubectl .
    • It is an api cluster resource stored in etcd, it is called ingress object
    • Ingress controller watches the ingress objects. It is deployed along with other pods as one among them like:
    Node A → App pod
       ↳ App pod
       ↳ nginx ingress controller pod
Node B → App pod
       ↳ App pod
    • Based on ingress object config, ingress controller manages the routing. -
  • namespaces:
    • means a boundary that keeps names from colliding
    • it is used for policy checks
      • Eg:
        • Resource Quota: Pod belongs to prod –> check prod quota
        • RBAC :- user accesses prod namespace –> check permissions
    • When we provide namespace to any manifest file, it creates multiple objects from that manifest file for each namespace.
  • stateful set
    • Most k8s workloads / pods are managed by a “Deployment” • But when a pod dies and when “Deployment” recreates the pod, the new pod recreates the pod, the IP & node can have suff name, IP & node. This is called stateless • This is generally used for- FE, API, servers, etc.
    • But some applications care about identity of the pods created & are not interchangable. In such case use “Stateful set”
    • Deployment pods look like api-6f84… etc, & every recreated pod gets a new name. stateful set pods look like postgres-1, postgres-2, etc out fixed names. each pod also gets a predictable pod name. This is very important for databases, distributed systems, cluster membership.
    • this works in association of persistent volume claim (PVC). Each pod gets its own storage which wont get destroyed when the pod gets destroyed. when a pod is recreated it attaches the same PVC as the older pod.
    • Ordered startup
      • In Deployment, “create 10 pods”, k8s may start them in parallel.
      • But stateful set starts in order: postgres-1 → postgres-2 → postgres-3, etc Similarly during shutdown, it stop db’s in reverse order.
      • this is because many distributed dbs require db 1 to start bt db2, b2 db 3, etc.
    • ordered updates
      • Pod deployment generally updates pods in batches. But Stateful set updates pods one after another. this is ordered rollout and generally useful for dbs.
    • stateful set components
      • when we apply “kind: StatefulSet” ; k8s creates a statefulset object stored in etcd. statefulset controller watches it. Statefulset controller then creates pods like postgres-1, postgres-2, etc based on the desired no. of pods mentioned in stateful set object being watched.
  • Daemonset
    • A k8s resource that ensures one copy of a pod runs on every matching node.
    • called daemonset because it is a set of
      • daemon-like pods running on nodes daemon → a background process that run continuously in background.
      • Example: we want to run a log collector on every node
      Node A → log collector
Node B → log collector
Node C → log collector
      • Deployment can’t guarantee this, it creates N replicas somewhere. (sometimes on one node)
      • But daemonset guarantees 1 pod per node.
      • Working:
        • We apply “kind: Daemonset”
        • kubectl reads the yaml file
        • API server authenticate
        • Daemonset object gets stored in etcd
        • Daemon controller watches daemon
        • By default it creates 1 pod per matching node.

        We cannot tell daemonset how many pods to sunper node. We can only say to run current pod in every node.

        • Eg of usage for :- kubeproxy, log controller, monitoring agents.
  • Job:
    • A k8s resource that tails, does same work
    • used for stuff like pdf generation, db migration
    • When deployment fails there is no further management as to retry or anything else. But when we configure job we can either retry or mark job as failed.
    • Can run parallel jobs
    • Flow:
      • Job obj stored in etcd
      • API server exposes it
      • Job controller watches Job obj
      • Job controller creates pod objects
      • Pod succeeds or fails Pod runs tasks
      • Job task succeeds go fails.
      • Job controller creates new pod if retry enabled, else marks Job as complete
      • Pod remain
  • CronJob:
    • K8s resource that creates job on schedule.
    • Create from CronJob manifest by kubectl & stored in etcd
    • CronJob controller watches CronJob via API server. When it is time, CronJob controller creates a Job obj.
    • Job controller creates job obj & creates a pod, Pod runs.
    • Pod succeed succeeds or fails. Retries if configured.
    • Job complete : Pods still remain
  • Secrets:
    • a K8s resource stored in etcd via terminal command for sake of safety. (bcz yaml file will record the secrets which we do not want)
    • We then reference the secrets obj name in deployment manifest, which will fetch the secrets directly from secrets obj. (eg: password)
  • Config map:
    • To store stuff like hostname, ports numbers, feature flags etc. (Non-sensitive data)
    • A K8s resource stored in etcd from manifest
  • Volume
    • Data storage
    • Specified as part of deployment manifest.
    • The actual data maybe stored within node/VM’s real disk or cloud or NFS (Network File system), but to the container it will look like it is coming from a folder within the container files.
    • Specification example: ```yaml volumes:
      • name: data mountPath: /data ```
    • It is specified as part of pod template in deployment manifest. When deployment controller creates pods each pod gets a volume named ‘data’. Just part of pod specification.
    • When pod is destroyed, the volume directly from container path will also be destroyed. When the directory gets destroyed, the associated actual db ins volume on disk also loses files in it.
    • Cons of volume per pod.
      • It is tied to pod life
      • Every pod will need to have volume specified
  • PV (Persistent volume) (Static Provisioning)
    • cluster level K8s obj stored in etcd created from PV manifest
    • Actual storage is on Node disk/cloud/NFS.
    • This object is created only for creating a… [continues to next page]
    • volume within the cluster for a ahead change in the volume, we use PVC.
    • Flow of creating PV volume in list
      • Fuse you create volume yourself.
      • Then just reference it in pv object. (This method is not used anymore)
  • PVC (Persistent Volume Claim):
    • Dynamic provisioning:
    • obj created from PVC manifest in etcd.
    • A storage controller notices PVC is pending & provisions storage.
    • eg: create EBS disk, GCP persistent disk, etc.
    • It then creates PV obj. & binds it to PVC (EBS, GCP disk, etc).
  • Node: Physical/virtual server.
  • Cluster: Group of physical datacenter servers.
  • Kube-system:
    • Namespace object stored in etcd.
    • created automatically during bootstap of control plane. (Eg: kubeadm init)
    • Part of other predefined yaml manifests
    • of system components : CoreDNS, kube-proxy, networking plugins (cni), etc.
    • Created by Namespace controller. It also creates default, kube system, kube public
    • Kube-node-lease:
    • Purpose: holds K8s internal components.
  • Sidecar:
    • Auxiliary container that runs inside same pod as main application & enhances or supports it.
    • has same network namespace (cannel, localhost shared), same storage volumes. (can be shared)
    • has separate process space (different container), separate lifecycle (can restart independently)
    • used to add functionality to or modifying main application code.
    • Eg:- logging, monitoring, proxying, security, configuration sync.
  • Init Containers:
    • temporary container that runs before main application
    • used to prepare env required by app (eg: wait for db/cache readiness, download config or secrets at runtime (sun DB migrations))
    • Not commonly used for smaller apps, but sahay for prod k8s systems, microservices
    • w/ dependencies, etc.
    • created from Pod yaml manifests.
    • spec -> initContainers -> Turns into pod object.
    • If initcontainers are omitted, pods start directly with containers
    • Developer defines it, K8s creates pod obj, kubelet executes based on pod objs.
  • Helm:
    • means ships steering wheel (k8s logo)
    • package manager for K8s. Bundles K8s yaml manifests into reusable, versioned packages called charts.
    • not a core component of cluster -> It is a cli tool on our m/c or CI/CD pipeline.
    • talks to K8s API server, applies manifests into cluster.
    • Without helm you need to manually manage multiple yaml files, repeated configs across envs, hard to version & reuse
    • Deployments:
      • with helm, everything is packaged, configurable via values, easy install/upgrade/rollback.
    • Helm Chart:
      • Chart
        • package K8s applicationist
        • contains templates values & chart yaml files
      • Template - K8s yaml templates
      • values.yaml - configurable params
      • chart.yaml - metadata (name, version)
    • Structure:
    my-chart/
|--- chart.yaml
|--- values.yaml
|--- templates
      |--> deployment.yaml
      |--> service.yaml
      |--> configmap.yaml
    • Working of helm:
      • You install a chart: helm install prometheus prometheus-community/prometheus
      • Helm renders templates: - replaces placeholders in yaml.
        • Eg: image: becomes image: prom/prometheus
      • Helm applies manifests:
        • helm sends final yaml to K8s API server
        • eg: deployment, service, configmap, ingress, etc.
      • K8s stores it in etcd like other normal resources.
    • Key features:
      • Allows install of packages called charts, like prometheus, grafana, nginx, ingress, postgresql.
      • Versioning/rollback supported: “helm rollback my-release 1”
      • Reusability: Same chart works across dev, staging, prod. Just change values.yaml.
      • Upgrade/update cluster resources safely: “helm upgrade my-app /chart”
    • Comparison of helm vs normal kubectl:
      • Without helm: use kubectl apply on every yaml file. No release history, nothing.
      • With helm: use helm install my-app name.
      • eg. internally it will pull templates yaml, values.yaml, generate less yaml. internally apply them (like kubectl), store release history.
  • Operator:
    • K8s extension that automates full lifecycle of complex applications using CRD (Custom Resource Definitions) & Custom Controllers (reconciliation logic).
    • It acts like a system administrator (“operator”)
    • In normal K8s, it can manage stateless apps (deployments), basic scaling (HPA), simple configs.
    • But it struggles with stateful, complex systems like Postgres databases, kafka cluster, elasticsearch, etc.
  • A cluster is multiple pods spun within same K8s cluster related to same application for complex purpose. Like :-
k8s
|--> nestjs Pod (Our own app)
|--> postgres-primary-------|
|--> postgres-replica-1     |---> postgres cluster
|--> postgres-replica-2-----|
  • CRD obj is stored in etcd
  • It is watched by operator controller. specific to the cluster we want (Postgres, kafka) . The cluster specific operator is installed in K8s cluster, via operator manifest in which in the deployment section, the location from/image from where the operator needs to be installed is mentioned. This installed operator will take care of replicas, replication, failure, backups, upgrades, etc.

Deployment section example in operator

kind: deployment
containers:
- image:
  Some-company
  postgres
  Operator: v1
  • CRD (Custom Resource Definition):
    • lets us add new resource type to K8s. (that are not built-in like kind:Pod, kind:Service, kind:Deployment, etc)
    • Examples for new resource types:
    • kind: kafkaCluster, kind: PostgresCluster
    • Added it is defined in operator manifest in CRD section, which only fully K8s that one specific type of obj exists.
    • The actual creation of object for that cluster is dependent on custom resource file (the manifest specific to that object)
    • eg. If CRD section in operator.yaml
    kind: CustomResourceDefinition
spec:
  names:
    kind: PostgresCluster
    • Custom Resource (CR) example
    postgres-cluster.yaml
kind: PostgresCluster
metadata:
  name: my-db
spec:
  instances: 3
  • API Group:
    • so when K8s is installed. kubeapi server comes along w/ it. In kube api server, along w/ it comes some built-in API (sources) - These APIs are exposed to outside K8s to which HTTP API calls are made by kubectl (http client)
    • API groups are some groupings made by K8s for these api paths for each resource type.
      • Built in API groups & paths:
        • CORE (no group) api/v1
          • pods, services, configmaps, secrets, nodes, namespaces
        • app. (/apps/apps/v1)
          • Deployments, Replicasets, Statefulsets, Daemonsets
        • batch (/apis/batch/v1)
          • Jobs, CronJobs
        • networking (/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1)
          • Ingress, NetworkPolicy
        • autoscaling (/apis/ /HPA) These all are compiled into kube-apiserver.
      • Additional APIs
        • Generate via CRDS.
        • kube-apiserver dynamically registers new route when user creates CRD.
        • we get new api path like apis/mycompany.com/v1/resources.
      • Aggregated API server (Advanced).
        • External API server can also plug into kube-api server.
      • Most of the conversations with K8s cluster between kubectl, kubelet, etc, controller schedules with kube-api server.happens via http/https rest & watch api calls & requests & these api paths
      • when writing manifest files, we mention the api path associated with its resource type so that kube-api server can do it like this :
        • apiVersion: apps/v1
          • kind: Deployment
        • apiVersion: v1
          • kind: Pod
        • apiVersion: batch/v1
          • kind: Job … etc
      • This is done so that when these manifests are applied, kube-api server can do the following:
        • Parse apiVersion + kind
        • Find matching resource handler
        • Validate schemas
        • Run admission controllers
        • Default missing fields
        • Store object in etcd
  • Admission Controllers
    • So when a request is made to K8s cluster via kubectl, a lot of stuff/checks happen w/ admission controllers are just part of it.
    • Stuff that happens after req from kubectl to kube-api server:
    kubectl apply deployment.yaml (via http req)
  |
  v
kube-api-server
|-- http routing (matches apiVersion = apps/v1, kind = Deployment)
|-- authentication(verify who is making the req)
|-- authorization(verify if authenticated user is allowed to make req)
|-- request decoders(convert manifest to resource obj)
|-- API resource lookup(kube finds appropriate handlers from
|     internal api-registry to handle [apps/v1, Deployment])Decoded resourceobj
|-- (built-in) Admission chain (chain of admission controllers)
    |-- service account controllers(injects default secure account)
    |-- default storage class(adds default storage class if omitted)
    |-- limit ranger (applies/enforces resource limits)
    |-- Pod security (checks security requirement)
    |-- resource quota (check namespace quota)
    |-- Mutating Admission Webhook (Calls custom mutation webhooks)
    |-- Validating Admission webhook (Calls custom validation webhooks)
    • Custom use defined admission controllers can also be added later via manifests.
  • Taints
    • rule applied to node based on which pods are not to be scheduled there. (cause normally all nodes are welcome to host pods).
    • Cases when you need to taint: GPU workloads, db workloads, infra components, control plane components.
    • How a taint looks like:
      • dedicated = database : NoSchedule
      • gpu = true : NoSchedule
    • Ways to taint nodes:
      • (Most common) kubectl taint kubectl taint nods worker-1 dedicated = gpu : NoSchedule
      • directly in Node manifest (less common).
      apiVersion : v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  name: worker-1
spec:
  taints:
  - key: dedicated
  value: gpu
  effect: NoSchedule
      • Automatically by K8s (some taints are added by controller)
      • e.g: node.kubernetes.io/not-readynode.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure … etc.
  • Tolerations
    • Rule on pod saying, allowing it to run on a node set not wanting taint.node set not wanting taint.
    • Defined in Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, Daemonset specification manifests.
    • e.g: 
      apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
template:
  spec:
    tolerations
    - key: dedicated
    operator: equal
    value: gpu
    effect: NoSchedule

      Not satisfying taint - toleration can make pods pending

    • e.g: 3 taint & toleration
      • Node 1 -> accept all pods (no taint)
      • Node 2 -> tainted (gpu=true:NoSchedule)
      • Pod 1 -> no toleration
      • Pod 2 -> toleration - gpu=true: noo schedule
      • Result:
        • Node 2 - Pod 2 allowed, pod 2 rejected
        • Node 1 - Pod 1 allowed, pod 2 allowed.
  • Affinity/Anti-affinity
    • Rules before allowing pods to be placed near/force from any node/pod.
    • Can have node affinity e.g: pod affinity/anti affinity.Can be hard/soft rules.Must have topology key.
    • Node affinity
      • pod placement based on node labels.
      • e.g: if
        • Node A - disk=ssd
        • Node B - disk=hdd
        • Then Pod - Node Affinity :- disk = ssd. Schedule onto SSD nodes.
    • Pod Affinity/AntiAffinity
      • Pod placement based on other pod labels.
    • Hard rule: Soft rules
      • Hard rule
        • must satisfy. Else pod state goes into pending.
      • Soft rule
        • nice to have. But pod will still run somewhere.
    • Topology key (Scope)
      • Region where pod must have affinity/anti-affinity.
      • Eg: Near xyz node. Near xyz zone… etc.
    • eg to all taint + toleration + affinities
    Cluster
|--Node A
|  |--labels:
|  |   type=gpu
|  |   zone=east
|  |--taint:
|      dedicated = gpu : NoSchedule.
|--Node B
|  |--labels:
|  |   type=general
|  |   zone=east
|  |--no taint.
|--Node C
   |--labels:
   |   type=gpu
   |   zone=west
   |--taint:
       dedicated = gpu : NoSchedule.

-> Existing pod
redis
|-- running on node A.
|--labels:
|--app=redis

-> New pod (api-server)
Tolerations:
- key: dedicated
  value: gpu
affinity:
  Node Affinity:
    required:
      type = gpu
  Pod Affinity:
    required:
      app = redis
  Pod AntiAffinity:
    required:
      app = api-server

-> Result:
Node taint -> all gpu tainted.
New pod toleration -> gpu taint. So can run on all nodes A, B, C.
Node affinity -> on nodes w/ type=gpu.
                So Node A ✓, Node B ×, Node C ✓
new pod, pod affinity -> near redis so Node A ✓, Node C ×
pod anti affinity -> Not near api-server.
                    Since no node has api-server pod, Node A ✓.
    • Case
      • If Node A had a pod for api-server, then new pod will go into pending state.
  • Eviction
    • K8s process of removing pod from Node. K8s pod would normally stop on its own.
    • Reasons: Memory pressure, Disk Pressure, Node failure, A node having taint called “No-execut” like maintenance = true. “NoExecute” like “maintenance = true? NoExecute
    • Eviction vs Deletion
      • Eviction done by k8s, Delete - user removal
      • User can also manually want it to evict via kubectl.
    • After eviction
      • If statefulset or deployment or replacement pod from evicted w/ new one created w/ out migration.
      • If standalone pod -> Pod evicted & Gone.
    • Evictions can be rejected by. Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) restricted.
      • Eg: minAvailable : 2
      • (keeps 2 replicas always healthy - Protection during maintenance).
    • Eviction Not same as OOM kill.
      • Eviction -> Done by k8s
      • OOMkill -> (out of memory kill) done by node.
  • Drain
    • Process of safely removing workloads from node.
    • Reasons: Reboot a VM, upgrade the OS, replace hardware, upgrade, kubelet; Shutdown node.
    • Process
      • marks pod mode as unschedulable.
      • evicts existing pods.
      • if deployment, the controller - recreate pods elsewhere & then evict.
      • After drain, safe to reboot, shutdown, etc.
    • Cordon vs Drain
      • cordon -> only marking node as unschedulable.
      • drain -> mark & evict.

        Uncordon -> unmark it as schedulable.

    • Daemonset Pods are generally ignored during drain in terminal command “kubectl drain worker-1 –ignore -daemonsets.”

Cluster diagram

Developer/User machine
|-- Developer laptop
| |-- kubectl
| |-- kubeconfig
| |-- Browser
|-- CI/CD machine
| |-- kubectl
| |-- helm
| |-- ArgoCD CLI
| |-- Deployment Pipelines
|-- Admin Machine
|-- kubectl
|-- kubeadm

K8s cluster
|-- Control Plane Nodes
| |-- kubelet
| |-- Static Pods
| | |-- kube-api-server Pod
| | |-- kube-scheduler Pod
| | |-- kube-controller-manager Pod
| | |-- etcd Pod
| |-- Container Runtime (containerd / CRI-O)
| |-- CNI components
| |-- CSI components
|-- Worker Nodes
| |-- kubelet
| |-- kube-proxy
| |-- Container Runtime (containerd / CRI-O)
| |-- CNI Components
| |-- CSI Node components
| |-- Pods
| |-- Application Pod
| |-- CoreDNS Pod
| |-- Metrics Server Pod
| |-- Ingress Controller Pod
| |-- Prometheus Pod
| |-- Grafana Pod
|-- K8s API objects (records stored in etcd)
|-- Namespace
|-- Node
|-- Pod
|-- ReplicationSet
|-- Deployment
|-- StatefulSet
|-- DaemonSet
|-- Job
|-- CronJob
|-- Ingress
|-- Ingress Class
|-- Gateway
|-- HttpRoute
|-- Config Map
|-- Secret
|-- Secure Account
|-- Persistent Volume
|-- Persistent Volume Claim
|-- Storage Class
|-- Service
|-- Endpoints
|-- EndpointSlice
|-- Resource Quota
|-- Limit Range
|-- Resource Quota
|-- Limit Range
|-- Network Policy
|-- Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
|-- Pod Disruption Budget
|-- Priority Class
|-- Runtime Class
|-- Custom Resource Definition
|-- Custom Resources

External Systems
|-- Container Registry (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR, Artifact Registry)
|-- DNS provider
|-- Storage System (NFS, Ceph, SAN, NAS)
|-- Cloud load balancer
|-- External users
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (K8s Structure and visualization Part 2)

entry.title: 03. K8s Basics
entry.content:
K8s Basics

So we are back to continuing with k8s basics dropping media forge in between 🥲🙂

Linux Basics

Back to understanding linux basics for k8s. They include processes, ports, networking, DNS, file systems, permissions, env variables, systemd, services, logs

  • Processes:
    • A combination of program instructions, memory used, CPU execution state, open files, network connections, security identity, env variables is called a process
    • Process handling in physical rack server
      • CPU core execute process instruction
      • RAM store process data
      • Disk (HDD/SSD) store process file
      • NIC/network card process network traffic (send and receives network packets)
      • Linux kernel schedue CPU time between processes

    • Physical rack visualization

      |-------------------------|
| CPU                     |
| RAM                     |
| SSD/HDD                 |
| NIC                     |
| |----------------|      |
| | Linux Kernel   |      |
| |----------------|      |
|-------------------------|
      • NIC
        • Network interface card
        • Hardware for network communication like via ethernet ports, fibre ports, wireless radio hardwood
      • VIsualization
      Nestjs app -----|
    |           |-----Application
    v           |
Socket API -----|
    |
    v
Linux Kernel Networking Stack
    |
    v
NIC driver -----------------|
    |                       |
    v                       |
NIC hardware                |------- Hardware to communicate via sockets
    |                       |
    v                       |
Ethernet cable/ network ----|
  • Ports:
    • Communication endpoint
    • Use ports to decide which process receives incoming n/w traffic
    • Kernel does forwarding of n/w from ports to its associated process
  • Networking
    • Just basic concepts of who connects by what
    • Eg: Ethernet cables/fiber connects server, cables connect to switches, etc
  • DNS (Domain Name System)
    • Converts domain names to IP address, via which servers communicate
  • File systems
    • organize data on storage systems
    • eg: SSD, HDD, etc
  • Permissions
    • Eg: -rwxr-x—
    • Rules followed in permissions: 
      `- rwx r-x r--`
 | |-| |-| |-|
 |  |   |   |
 |  |   |   v
 |  |   |   other permission
 |  |   v
 |  |   group permission
 |  v
 |  owner permission
 v
 Filetype
    • filetype
      • -: regular file
      • d: directory
      • l: symbolic link
    • permissions - r read, w write, x execute, - no permission
    • Numeric representation
      • r - 4
      • w - 2
      • x - 1
      • rwx - 7
      • r-x - 5
      • --- - 0
      • - rwx r-x r-- - 750
      • Can be used as "chmod 750 filename"
  • Env variable - As we know it
  • systemd / services
    • systemd
      • linux service manager
      • controls starting, stopping, restarting services, etc.
      • eg services -> nginx, ssh, docker, etc.
      • command -> "systemctl status"
  • Logs - As we know it

Containers

Images, containers, layers, volumes, networks, entrypoints, env variables, multi stage builds.

  • Images
    • packaged filesystem
    • metadata used to create container
    • contains application files, libraries, runtime binaries, default config, startup command.
    • readonly templates
    • when container starts
      • mount image filesystem
      • add a writable layer
        • copy files from readonly to writable files & run from there
      • start process
  • Container Runtime
    • eg: docker, containerd
    • creates containers (processes from image), configure namespaces/cgroup, mount filesystem, set networking, start process
  • Container
    • Process made from image
    • Eg: running “docker run redis”..
      • creates redis process
      • creates isolated filesystem
      • creates virtual n/w interface
      • creates writable container layer
  • Layers
    • something with which images are built.
    • each Dockerfile instruction creates a build tor file/file/folder, that is a new filesystem layer.
    • Each tor file/folder created is immutable, and each of them is called a layer.
    • Container stacks them using OverlayFS (a linux filesystem tech that allows multiple directories/filesystems to be stacked together into one unified filesystem view).
  • Volumes
    • Persistent storage for containers outside container lifecycle.
  • Networks
    • Docker creates virtual networking using:
      • linux bridges
      • Virtual Ethernet interfaces (Veth)
      • NAT rules
      • routing tables
    • Linux bridge:
      • virtual software switch to which containers connect to; called “docker0”
      • created by docker.
      • Visualisation
      `container A` ---\
`container B` ----> `"docker0" bridge --> `Host NIC` --> `Internet`
`container C` ---/
      • Part of virtual network interfaces
    • Virtual Ethernet interfaces (Veth pair)
      • created by docker during container start
      • called as “virtual cable pair” (veth pair)
      • part of virtual network interfaces.
      • has one side inside container (eth0), one side outside container (veth7abc123)
      • visualisation: 
        container eth0 <--- virtual cable ---> host veth xyz
    • NAT rules (Network Address Translation)
      • Networking Address Translation rules
      • Rules/Instructions to how packets (that travel through sys) must be rewritten.
      • This rewriting allows containers w/ private IPs to access host’s internet via host IP (translation).
      • Rules exist because not every packet must be translated.
      • Eg commands: SNAT, DNAT, MASQUERADE, REDIRECT.
      • This is not just of docker but of host system, linux in general, VPN, etc too. (used everywhere for rewriting packet addresses)
      • It is a subset rule among many other rules in linux iptables.
        • ip-table
          • tool/sys/networking/firewall utility.
          • iptable defines what happens to packets.
          • used for managing packet rules.
          • eg:
          iptables
|--- filter rules
|--- forwarding rules
|--- logging rules
|--- NAT rules
          • eg of iptable rules:
            • Allow incoming SSH traffic
            • Rewrite packet source IP.
            • . . . etc
          • Answers questions like allow packet?, block packet?, rewrite IP?, forward IP?, log packet?
    • Routing Tables
      • Answers questions like where to hop next, which network interface should transmit the packet, etc.
      • decides where the packets go to.
      • In terms of docker, this decides which packets go to that container related packets go to docker0 (linux bridge), while internet traffic go to router etc.
  • Entry Points
    • main command started when container launches.
    • Eg: ENTRYPOINT [“node”, “server.js”]
    • When the process marked as entrypoint (here it is “node server.js”), it becomes PID 1 process.
  • Env Variables (same we know it)
  • Multi stage builds
    • We can have multiple stages in dockerfile by writing like this - “FROM xyz as abc”.
    • Generally all commands in dockerfile creator makes one layer.
    • All layers all together makes one stage.
    • And this stage builds itself to create one image which is referenced by docker to run in the container.
    • With multistage builds, only the final stage is referenced as the image created by the dockerfile
    • During each stage in multistage builds, multiple stages (few stage images / temporary stages) are created (collection of layer files) and stored in disk. But only final stage image is exposed to docker & becomes the o/p.
    • Benefit : smaller containers, faster deployments, reduced attack surface, lower memory/storage usage.

Purpose of K8s

Problem and their solutions via k8s

  • Container crashes —> self healing
    • w/o containers K8s, need to manually up stuff
    • K8s continuously watches containers
    • w/ containers K8s, RAM etc re-allocation, filesystem remounting, network interface recreation etc is taken care of.
  • multiple server -> scheduling
    • K8s simplifies scheduling pods into free servers w/o having to manually track it via scheduler
  • Traffic routing -> services
    • K8s services allow having stable traffic routing to healthy BE pods w/o manually having to handle it.
  • Scaling -> Replica Set via Services
    • Distribution of load across back servers automatically done by K8s w/o manual intervention under higher load via ReplicaSet
  • Config management -> configmaps / Secrets
    • Diff env config & secrets injected into container memory w/o rebuilding using K8s.
  • Deployments -> Rolling updates
    • Updates applications w/o downtime via K8s.
    • Process: — start new pod, wait until healthy, stop old pod, repeat gradually.
  • Service discovery -> DNS
    • K8s provides internal DNS to communicate set of pods even when they move frequently b/w back servers.
    • Process: — Application attempts to DNS lookup, req sent through DNS Virtual n/w, cluster DNS responds, app server receives current service IP.
  • Resource Control -> Requests / limits
    • To avoid applns from competing for hardware resources, we can set request limits & limits for cpu, memory, etc in k8s deployment manifest (or any other manifest that has deployment spec). This set hardware resource limits on containers (not on pod or node).
  • Receiving K8s Architecture First
    • Cluster
      • group of physical/virtual servers working together to run applications
      • Consists of control plne and worker nodes
    • Control plane
      • management brain of K8s.
      • doesn’t normally run an appln container
      • Responsibilities :- accept requests, store cluster state, make decisions, monitor cluster status, command worker nodes.
    • API server
      • front door of K8s (and through it)
      • Everything talks to it :- kubectl, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet - Responsibilities — validate req, authenticate user, authorize action, store resource obj.
    • etcd
      • K8s db. Stores cluster state
      • Also writes to physical storage devices (CRI, CSI, etc)
    • scheduler
      • decides which node the pod must go to.
      • a process running on control plane
    • Controller manager
      • continuously check desired state vs actual state
      • a process on control plane that keeps doing - observe, compare, correct (called as reconciliation loop).
      • reason why K8s correct itself
    • kubelet
      • agent running on every worker node.
      • receives instruction from control plane
      • ensures containers are running
    • Container runtime
      • runtime that actually runs containers
      • eg: containerd, CRI-O
      • Process :- Pull required image, create filesystem, configure networking, start process
    • kube proxy
      • manage n/w rules for services.
      • when traffic arrives at a service, kube proxy routes it to correct pod based on iptables / networking rules.

Most important K8s concept (Desired state reconciliation)

  • Desired state reconciliation
    • We declare desired state (eg: replicas 3) and K8s try to match it to reality via reconciliation loops
  • Self healing
    • basically reconciliation fixing failures
    • cluster repairing itself
  • Auto recreation
    • K8s automatically recreates missing resources
    • Eg: Someone manually deletes a pod. But desired state says it needs 3 replicas, & reality has only 2 pods, so controller immediately creates another pod.
  • Controllers
    • software that perform reconciliation
    • Reconciliation loop :- controller continuously watching, comparing, acting & repeating
    • A linux process running on control plane service
  • Deployments
    • stores desired appln state
      (deployment is the instruction, controllers perform the instruction)
  • Scaling
    • changing desired capacity
    • eg: from replica: 3 to replica: 10
  • Rollback
    • change desired state to prev version

Learn Objects

  • Phase 1 - Pods
    • what:
      • smallest deployable unit in K8s.
      • The thing that k8s schedules into worker nodes
      • contains >= 1 containers
      • not a process itself.
      • a K8s object that run & manages the process (aka :- container)
      • pod & container :-
        • pod = wrapper
        • container = isolated process env
        pod

container A         container B
|-------------|     |-------------|
| process A   |     | process B   |
|-------------|     |-------------|
        • a pod provides shared n/w, shared storage, shared lifecycle.
        • multi containers Pods - pods can have multiple containers
        • pod lifecycle Green
          • Pending -> Pod created, image downloading, waiting for node.
          • running -> containers started, app “running”
          • Failed -> container crashed - pod failed
        • logs — “kubectl logs my-pod”
        • Exec into pod :
          • “kubectl exec -it my-pod – sh”
          • allows to start a command inside a running container.
  • Phase 2 — Deployment
    • Replica set - ensure specific no. of pods exist
    • Scaling - Change no. of pod replicas
    • Rolling updates - update application version gradually
    • Rollback - revert back version
  • Phase 3 — Service
    • Service - Provides a reliable n/w endpoint for pods
    • Cluster IP :
      • IP for internal cluster communication.
      • So that traffic remains inside cluster networking & no external traffic reaches it.
    • Nodeport — port used to expose a service through a worker node’s IP.
      — can be accessed from outside cluster cluster IP
      — common uses includes connecting external load balancers, for development & testing quickly.
      • expose app “1010 DNS or load balancers, etc.
      • Eg for NodePort & Node IP. “http://Node-IP:30050”
      • worker node listens to this TCP port.
    • Load balancer
      • for exposing services externally. & forward traffic to cluster nodes
    • Service discovery
      • Service discovery is done via service names
      • It is done so that pods can move around w/o breaking communication
      • A service can point to multiple pods like redis-service can have multiple replicas of pods, but all can be accessed by same name.
    • kube-dns/coredns — DNS server K8S
      • just another pod running on worker node CPU’s & RAM
    • Label selectors — labels used for services to find pods
      • Eg: 
        Pod
"label:
    app: backend"
Service
"selector:
    app: backend"

        Now K8S matches them.

      • labels are metadata stored in it.cd
  • Phase 4 — Configmap & Secrets
    • Env variable injection
      • Eg: Config map contain env variables, containers can access them inside process env.[var-name]
    • Mounted files
      • Provide config as files instead of env variables
      • Eg: Config map has app.conf. It is mounted in containers as /etc/config/app.conf
      • to app “it looks like normal file on disk”
      • (means file contents become visible inside filesystem namespace, just like a normal file).
    • Separation of config from image
      — container image is kept independent from configuration
      — ie, when config changes per namespace like diff for prod & dev, the image of container is unaffected.
    • Secrets
      • store sensitive config
      • consumed as env variables or mounted files.
  • Phase 5 — Ingress
    • Reverse proxy — receive req & forward it to execution
      • Ingress controller: is a process running on worker node CPUs.
      • Eg: user requests at https://example.com ingress receives it & forwards it to frontend-service.
    • Routing — a thing that reverse proxy does.
      • deciding which service gets the incoming req.
    • Domain name — human readable names created from Service names instead of IP addresses.
      • DNS resolves the domain to the ingress endpoint
      • Traffic then flows through switches, routers, NICs, and into the cluster
    • TLS termination — handle HTTPS encryption
      — TLS = Transport layer security.
      — Ingress terminates TLS (stops encrypted traffic & decrypts it by security)
      • it decrypts & forwards the req internally.
    • NGINX ingress controller
      • perform the ingress functionality based on ingress obj stored in etcd.
  • Phase 6 — Storage
    • Volumes — provide storage to pods
      — Volume ultimately resides on SSD, NVMe (solid state device), NVMe, & HDD, n/w storage
    • Persistent Volume (PV) — declares/represents actual storage available to the cluster.
    • Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)
      • Storage requested by pods
      • Eg: Pod requests “I need 50GB”. K8S find a matching PV & binds Pod & PV. Pod don’t care which disk provides the storage.
    • Stateful Workloads
      • Apps / Pods which are not stateless
      • Eg: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, redis
      • When these pods restart, the process change from old to new container, but same volume/storage is used.
  • Phase 6 — Networking Fundamentals
    • Pod net networking
      • Every pod gets its own IP & each one communicates to other via these IPs.
      • Packets of data need to travel through these to reach from one pod to another via network :-
        Pod 1 - VETH (virtual n/w interface) - worker node NIC - switch - other worker node - destination pod.
    • Service virtual IPs
      • Eg: “backend-service”
      • stable addresses for a group of pods.
    • kube-proxy — routing btw pods internally based on service names.
      • it also configures networking rules on every worker node.
    • CNI plugin
      • Container Networking Interface
      • Create Pod networking.
      • Process of CNI working (what all CNI does)
        • when a new pod starts
          • CNI allocates an IP
          • create network interface
          • configure routing
          • connect pod to cluster N/W.
      • Points to note:
        • CNI (container n/w interface) is a specification, by a set of plugins.
        • it creates/configures n/working for containers & pods.
        • CNI plugin is a plugin that resides on every K8s node. It is an executable file. unlike API objects or controllers, which create/configure upon running the file.
        • It doesn’t generally come with K8s cluster when we create one. A ductii controllers and such. A administrator generally need to set it up.
        • Commonly installed CNI plugins :- Calico, Cilium, Flannel. Page 2(2)
        • But many providers provide auto installs, many things for developers thus it may feel like built in.
        • Providers that auto installs include :- minikube kind, EKS, GKE, AKS. DNS Resolution - convert name into IP addresses.
  • Phase 7 - Resource management
    • Requests :
      • to declare minimum resources required (pod-level)
      • eg: 
        requests:
cpu: 500m
memory: 512Mi
      • this means: pods node needs 0.5 CPU & 512 MB RAM.
    • Limits :
      • to declare maximum resources allowed.
      • eg: 
        limits:
cpu : 1
memory : 1Gi
      • which means node needs max 1 CPU & 1 GB RAM

        For nodes, resources are allocated via “capacity” and “allocatable resources” To decide placement of pods in nodes, scheduler adds the requests & limits of pods/containers & then compares with node allocatable capacity

    • cpu throttling
      • Prevent containers from exceeding CPU limits
      • Process :
        • Developer sets CPU limit 
          limits :
cpu : 1"
        • kubelet reads pod spec.
        • Container runtime configures cgroups.
          • runtime creates linux cgroup setting for container
        • linux kernel tracks cpu usage by watching how much CPU time certain cgroup consumes.
        • Container reaches its quota C like if cpu is 1; but container consumes 100ms of cpu time (quota) every 100 ms window (period).
        • Kernel throttles.
          • kernel blocks further cpu execution. Container waits until the next period begins. (means process is either killed nor pod is contacted. Process sleeps.)
      • OOM killed
        • out of memory killed
        • purpose is to protect node from memory exhaustion
        • When RAM usage exceeds by containers, kernel kills the containers process. Then the pod may be restarted

          Note
          cpu limit exceed -> process only steps (Throttle)
          memory limit exceed -> process killed (oom)

      • scheduling
        • K8s scheduler choosing which node will run the pod.
      • Node Pressure:
        • Purpose is to detect overloaded nodes
        • Common pressure types: Memory pressure, disk pressure, PID pressure.
        • e.g. K8s servers have RAM = 128 GB, used RAM = 127 GB
          • node enters memory pressure
          • K8s may evict nodes to protect the node.

            If no free nodes 10% full memory exists on the cluster, then the Page 5exists on the cluster, then the new pod goes into pending state (In case of fixed replicaset with stateless deployment pods)
entry.summary: Intro to kubernetes (K8s Basics)

entry.title: OOP
entry.content:
• Mental model

    • OOP - thinknig in objects
    • LLD - designing system using OOP
    • HLD - scaling those systems



  • Thinking in objects

    • Q. Design a library system
    • Steps:
      • Identify entities: Book, User, Library, Transaction (* OOP is not about classes, but rather about modelling real world entities)
      • Develop Reponsisbilty thinking:
        • Book: knows title, author, availability
        • User: can borrow books
        • Transaction: tracks borrow/return
        • Library: manages books
  • Q. Online food ordering sysytem. List entities and give 1 responsibility per entity
    • Tips:

      • Keep it modelling-heavy and less of list-heavy

      • Do not mix levels of abstraction (eg: ingrdients is very low level, orders is core domain, offers is an optional feature, employees is an internal sysytem detail). In interview it will look like candidate is listing everything instead of structuring the domain

      • Non negotiable core entities: User, Restaurant, Menu, Order, Payment
      • Supporting entities: Delivery Agent, Location, Review, Offer (optional)
      • Reponsibilities:
        • User: place order, view order
        • Restaurant: manage menu, process order
        • Order: calculate total, update status
        • Payment: handle transaction
        • Menu: provide items

    • How to identitfy primary actors and itheri associated entities:

      • Identify the target users
        • They are teh first class actors
        • eg: Customer, Restaurant owner, delivery agent
      • Identfy the enitities facing them
        • They are the high level entities
        • eg:
          • Cutomer -> browse(menu), order, pay
          • restaurant -> manage menu, accet orders
          • delivery agent -> deliver orders
